paragraphs: When the protocol had been signed, Nikolay Parfenovitch turned solemnly to the prisoner and read him the “Committal.” It set out that in such a year, on such a day, in such a place, the investigating lawyer of such-and-such a district court had examined so-and-so (namely, Mitya), accused of this and of that (all the charges were carefully written out). It noted that the accused did not plead guilty to the charges against him and had offered nothing in his defense, while the witnesses, so-and-so and so-and-so, and the circumstances, such-and-such, spoke against him. Acting under such-and-such articles of the Statute Book, and so on, the lawyer had ruled that, to prevent so-and-so (Mitya) from any means of evading pursuit and judgment, he be held in such-and-such a prison. He hereby notified the accused of this and sent a copy of the same “Committal” to the deputy prosecutor, and so on, and so on.

In short, Mitya was told that from that moment he was a prisoner, that he would be driven into town at once, and that he would be shut up there in a very unpleasant place. Mitya listened closely and only shrugged his shoulders.
“All right, gentlemen, I don’t hold it against you. I’m ready.... I see you have no other choice.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch told him gently that the rural police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, who happened to be on the spot, would escort him at once....
“Stay,” Mitya broke in suddenly. A feeling he could not hold back swept him along, and he spoke to everyone in the room:

“Gentlemen, we’re all cruel, we’re all monsters, we all make men weep, and mothers, and babes at the breast. But let it be settled here, now: of all of us, I am the lowest reptile! I swore to reform, and every day I’ve gone on doing the same filthy things. I understand now that men like me need a blow, a blow of destiny to catch them like a noose and bind them by a force from outside. Never, never would I have risen by myself! But the thunderbolt has fallen. I accept the torture of the accusation and my public shame. I want to suffer, and by suffering I will be purified. Perhaps I will be purified, gentlemen? But listen, for the last time: I am not guilty of my father’s blood. I accept my punishment, not because I killed him, but because I meant to kill him, and I might really have killed him. Still, I mean to fight it out with you. I warn you of that. I’ll fight it out with you to the end, and then God will decide. Good-by, gentlemen. Don’t be angry with me for shouting at you during the examination. Oh, I was such a fool then.... In another minute I’ll be a prisoner, but now, for the last time, as a free man, Dmitri Karamazov offers you his hand. In saying good-by to you, I say it to all men.”

His voice shook and he held out his hand. But Nikolay Parfenovitch, who happened to be standing nearest to him, made a sudden, almost nervous movement and hid his hands behind his back. Mitya noticed it instantly and started. He let his outstretched hand drop at once.

“The preliminary inquiry isn’t over yet,” Nikolay Parfenovitch faltered, rather embarrassed. “We’ll continue it in town, and I, for my part, of course, am ready to wish you every success ... in your defense.... The fact is, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I’ve always been inclined to see you, so to speak, as more unfortunate than guilty. All of us here, if I may be so bold as to speak for all, are ready to acknowledge that you are, at bottom, a young man of honor, but, alas, one who has been carried away by certain passions a little too far....”

By the time he had finished, Nikolay Parfenovitch’s little figure looked positively majestic. Mitya had the thought that in another minute this “boy” would take him by the arm, lead him off to another corner and start up their talk about “girls” again. But all sorts of irrelevant, out-of-place thoughts will come into a man’s head, even a prisoner’s, as he is being led out to execution.
“Gentlemen, you’re kind, you’re humane. Could I see _her_ and say ‘good-by’ one last time?” asked Mitya.
“Of course, but given that ... the truth is, now it can’t be done except in the presence of—”
“Oh, well, if it must be so, it must!”
Grushenka was brought in, but the farewell was brief, said in few words, and did not satisfy Nikolay Parfenovitch at all. Grushenka bowed low to Mitya.
“I told you I am yours, and I will be yours. I will follow you forever, wherever they send you. Farewell. You are innocent, though you’ve been your own ruin.”
Her lips quivered, and tears flowed from her eyes.
“Forgive me, Grusha, for my love, for ruining you, too, with my love.”

Mitya would have said more, but he broke off and went out. Men who kept constant watch on him at once surrounded him. At the foot of the steps, where he had driven up so dashingly the day before with Andrey’s three horses, two carts stood ready. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a sturdy, thick-set man with a wrinkled face, was annoyed about something, some sudden mix-up. He was shouting angrily. He told Mitya to get into the cart, with rather excessive surliness.

“The man had a very different face when I was standing him drinks at the tavern,” thought Mitya as he climbed in. A crowd had gathered at the gates: peasants, women, drivers. Trifon Borissovitch came down the steps as well. Everyone stared at Mitya.
“Forgive me at parting, good people!” Mitya suddenly shouted from the cart.
“Forgive us too!” he heard two or three voices say.
“Good-by to you, too, Trifon Borissovitch!”

But Trifon Borissovitch did not even turn around. Perhaps he was too busy. He, too, was shouting and fussing about something. It turned out that the second cart, in which two constables were to go along with Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, was not yet ready. The peasant who had been ordered to drive it was pulling on his smock, stubbornly insisting that it was not his turn to go but Akim’s. But Akim was nowhere to be seen. They ran to look for him. The peasant dug in his heels and begged them to wait.

“See what our peasants are like, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch? No shame at all!” exclaimed Trifon Borissovitch. “Akim paid you twenty-five copecks the day before yesterday. You drank it all, and now you start yelling. I’m simply astonished at how good-natured you are, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, with our low peasants. That’s all I can say.”
“But why do we need a second cart?” Mitya put in. “Let’s just set off in this one, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. I won’t make trouble, I won’t run away from you, old fellow. What’s the escort for?”

“I’ll thank you to learn how to speak to me, if nobody’s ever taught you. I’m not ‘old fellow’ to you, and you can keep your advice for another time!” Mavriky Mavrikyevitch snapped savagely, as though glad to vent his anger.

Mitya fell silent. He flushed all over. A moment later he suddenly felt very cold. The rain had stopped, but the dull sky was still covered with clouds, and a keen wind was blowing straight in his face.
“I’ve caught a chill,” thought Mitya, twitching his shoulders.

At last Mavriky Mavrikyevitch got into the cart too, sat down heavily, and, as though without noticing, squeezed Mitya into the corner. True, he was in a foul mood and greatly disliked the job that had been given him.
“Good-by, Trifon Borissovitch!” Mitya shouted again, and he felt himself that this time he had not called out from good nature, but involuntarily, from resentment.
But Trifon Borissovitch only stood there with an air of pride, both hands clasped behind him. He stared straight at Mitya, his face stern and angry, and gave no answer.
“Good-by, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, good-by!” Suddenly he heard Kalganov’s voice. Kalganov had dashed out and run up to the cart, and he held out his hand to Mitya. He had no cap on.
Mitya had time to seize and press his hand.
“Good-by, dear fellow! I won’t forget your generosity,” he cried warmly.
Then the cart lurched forward and their hands came apart. A bell began to ring, and Mitya was driven away.

Kalganov ran back, sat down in a corner, bent his head, hid his face in his hands and burst out crying. He sat like that for a long while, crying like a little boy instead of a young man of twenty. Oh, he believed almost without a doubt in Mitya’s guilt.
“What kind of people are these? What can men be after this?” he cried out incoherently, in bitter despondency, close to despair. At that moment he did not want to live.
“Is it worth it? Is it worth it?” cried the boy in his grief.
